questions.question: Henry Walter Bates spent nearly eleven years collecting insects in the Amazon rainforest. Birds there leave alone the boldly patterned butterflies of one group, which taste foul. Bates found that a few butterflies of a quite different family, which birds can eat safely, looked almost exactly like them. How does that likeness protect the look-alikes?
questions.answer: Birds that learned to shun the foul kind shun them too
choices: Birds that learned to shun the foul kind shun them too
Birds sickened by the foul kind give up eating butterflies
Birds are startled by the pattern and let them go
Birds cannot pick them out among the bright flowers
questions.context: A young bird that once bites a foul-tasting butterfly learns to avoid its pattern, so it passes over the harmless look-alikes as well: mimicry, a structural adaptation of colouring. The birds shun that one pattern, not every butterfly, and a bold pattern does not hide a butterfly but makes it easy to see. The trick works only while the look-alikes stay rarer than the foul kind, or birds would learn that the pattern means a meal.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.13C; curriculum line G8.L3) teaches colouring, camouflage and mimicry as structural adaptations, and Bates's butterflies are the classic case of mimicry.

questions.question: Scarlet kingsnakes are harmless, but their red, yellow and black rings look much like those of the venomous coral snake. David Pfennig's team set out 1,200 plasticine snakes in the Carolinas, some ringed like kingsnakes and others striped or plain brown. Some went where coral snakes live, and some farther north, where none do. Predators' bites left marks in the soft models. What did the marks show about the rings?
questions.answer: They protect only where coral snakes live
choices: They protect only where coral snakes live
They protect wherever the kingsnakes live
They draw attacks where coral snakes live
They make no difference to the predators
questions.context: Where coral snakes live, only about 6 percent of the attacks fell on ringed models; farther north, where there are none, about half did. Predators that have learned to fear a coral snake spare its look-alikes, but where no coral snake has taught that lesson the rings give no protection. The same colouring that saves a kingsnake in one place does nothing for it in another, just as Bates's idea of mimicry predicts.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.13C; NGSS MS-LS4-4) teaches that whether a trait helps depends on the environment, and the kingsnake models are the field experiment that shows it for mimicry.

questions.question: Arthur DeVries went to Antarctica in 1961 as a graduate student to study fish that live in seawater about 1.9 degrees Celsius below zero, cold enough to freeze most fishes' blood. With Donald Wohlschlag he found that the salts and other small substances in the Antarctic fishes' blood could account for only about half of its protection against freezing. Much of the rest came from a protein built with sugars. How does such a protein keep the blood from freezing?
questions.answer: It binds to tiny ice crystals and stops them growing
choices: It binds to tiny ice crystals and stops them growing
It makes heat that keeps the blood above freezing
It lets the blood freeze solid and thaw unharmed
It stops cold seawater from soaking into the body
questions.context: Tiny ice crystals get into the fish with its food and through its gills, and the antifreeze protein sticks to them so they cannot grow, keeping the blood liquid below its usual freezing point. It is a physiological adaptation, worked by the body's own chemistry; the protein makes no heat. Freezing solid and thawing out again is a different animal's way, the wood frog's.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.L3; TEKS 8.13C) teaches physiological adaptations, the body's own chemistry at work, and the antifreeze of polar fish is one of the standard examples.

questions.question: Raymond Cowles and Charles Bogert spent four years taking the body temperatures of lizards and snakes in a scorching California desert, and reported in 1944. Lizards were thought of as cold-blooded, their bodies simply as warm or as cool as their surroundings. The two men found that an active lizard kept its body near a temperature that suited it, while the ground baked by day and cooled at night. How did the lizards manage it?
questions.answer: By moving between sunshine, shade and burrows
choices: By moving between sunshine, shade and burrows
By sweating to cool their skin in the heat
By shivering to warm their muscles when cool
By burning extra food to make their own heat
questions.context: A lizard makes little heat of its own, so it basks and turns toward the Sun when cool and slips into shade or a burrow when too hot: control of body temperature by behaviour. Sweating, shivering and burning food for heat are the physiological ways of birds and mammals, and a reptile's dry, scaly skin has no sweat glands. Cowles proposed the words ectothermic and endothermic for the two groups.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.L3) teaches control of body temperature as an adaptation, and that it can be behavioural (basking, seeking shade) or physiological (sweating, shivering).

questions.question: Some desert rodents lose very little water in their urine, because their kidneys can make it up to about five times as concentrated as a person's kidneys can. Biologists sort adaptations into three kinds: structural, behavioural and physiological. Which kind of adaptation is this, and why?
questions.answer: Physiological, since it is the way an organ works
choices: Physiological, since it is the way an organ works
Structural, since the kidneys are parts of the body
Behavioural, since it lets the animal drink less
Structural, since the animal is born with it
questions.context: The kidneys are body parts, but the adaptation is what they do: they save water by making the urine concentrated, an inner working of the body, so it is physiological. The same rodents' habit of spending the hot day in a cool burrow is behavioural, and their fur is structural. All three kinds are inherited, so being born with a trait does not settle which kind it is.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.13C) asks students to sort adaptations into structural, behavioural and physiological kinds, and concentrated urine is a textbook physiological example.

questions.question: A desert rattlesnake has three adaptations for catching rodents: blotchy scales in the colours of the ground, venom that it injects through hollow fangs, and a habit of lying still in ambush where rodents pass. Biologists sort adaptations as structural, behavioural or physiological. How do they sort these three, in order?
choices: Structural, physiological, behavioural
Structural, structural, behavioural
Physiological, structural, behavioural
Structural, behavioural, behavioural
questions.context: The blotchy colouring is part of the snake's build, so it is structural, like any camouflage. Venom is a chemical made in the snake's venom glands, so it is physiological, even though the fangs that deliver it are structural. Lying in wait is something the snake does, so it is behavioural.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.13C) has students sort new examples into the three kinds, and a teaching guide for the standard gives snake venom as its physiological example.

questions.question: Rock pocket mice in the deserts of the American Southwest are mostly sandy brown, but on dark lava flows nearly all of them are black. Michael Nachman and Hopi Hoekstra found that the black mice on one lava flow carry changes in a single gene for coat colour. Black mice on another flow, hundreds of miles away, have no changes in that gene. What does this show?
questions.answer: Black coats arose separately on the two flows
choices: Black coats arose separately on the two flows
Black coats spread from one flow to the other
Black coats come from the dark rock, not from genes
Black coats on the second flow are not inherited
questions.context: Two different genetic routes to the same black coat mean it arose twice, each time from chance changes that some mice inherited and passed on, because owls and other hunters that hunt by sight pick off pale mice on dark rock. The mice on the second flow inherit their colour too, through changes in other genes. Mutations happen by chance, but selection does not: the same conditions favoured the same adaptation twice.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.13C; NGSS MS-LS4-4) teaches that adaptations grow out of inherited variation, and the rock pocket mouse is the standard middle-school case (HHMI's film).

questions.question: Snowshoe hares turn white each autumn and brown each spring. Marketa Zimova, L. Scott Mills and their team followed nearly 200 radio-collared hares in Montana. The hares began to change on about the same dates every year, however early or late the snow came, and hares left white on bare brown ground were killed more often. What sets off a hare's change of coat?
questions.answer: The changing length of the day
choices: The changing length of the day
The first snow of the autumn
The colour of the ground around it
The amount of food it can find
questions.context: Biologists think day length starts the change, and warmer winters do not alter the length of the days. So when snow comes late or melts early, hares turn white, or stay white, on bare ground, and the mismatched hares' weekly chance of survival fell by up to 7 percent. A colouring that hid them in the old world gives them away in a changed one, and only natural selection on the hares' inherited variation in timing can mend the mismatch.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (NGSS MS-LS4-4; curriculum line G8.L3) teaches that a trait helps only in the environment it suits, and the hares' camouflage mismatch is a measured case of a trait meeting a changed world.

questions.question: Blackcaps, small songbirds that nest in central Europe, once flew southwest each autumn to winter around Spain. From about 1960 a few began flying northwest to Britain instead, where garden bird tables offer food in winter, and within about thirty years several thousand wintered there. Peter Berthold raised young birds of both groups in identical cages in Germany, and each tried to head the way its own parents had flown. How did the new route spread?
questions.answer: Birds with the new heading thrived and passed it on
choices: Birds with the new heading thrived and passed it on
Young birds learned the way by following older ones
Garden food changed the birds' genes for direction
Each bird picked the route with the most food that year
questions.context: Young birds raised alike still headed their own parents' way, so the heading is inherited: a behavioural adaptation carried in the genes, and the young of crossed parents headed about halfway between. Selection favoured the birds that wintered in Britain, so the northwest heading spread over the generations. Food does not rewrite a bird's genes, and a route picked afresh each year would not follow the parents.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.13C) teaches migration as a behavioural adaptation that grows out of inherited variation over generations, and the blackcaps' new route is a case measured within living memory.
